subject: The inspector general’s file at Justice

locus.descriptor: the White House counsel’s room with the inspector general’s open notice on the table

context.standing: The Justice Department inspector general has opened a private audit into {{matterSubject}}. The office is still gathering its first record. The President can act on Justice, but cannot decide what the inspector general finds.
context.precedent: A case-specific presidential instruction to Justice can be refused under the department’s communication rules. A broader enforcement posture can be carried without directing this audit. Written notice to remove an inspector general takes thirty days, leaves the audit running, and makes the obstruction public.

pressures.want: The Attorney General warns that an order to investigate this audit’s subject can be refused as case direction from the White House.
Congress has not yet heard of the audit. A removal notice would put both the inquiry and the President’s move against it before members.
White House counsel says a department-wide enforcement instruction must not be sold as an answer to the inspector general’s own file.
The audit is still private. The President’s written removal notice would make the struggle over it a public matter.

context.inaction: The inspector general continues the private audit. Justice receives no new presidential directive, and the inspector general stays in office.
context.unknown: The audit has not reported a finding. Justice may refuse a case-specific instruction, and no one can say yet what the inspector general will conclude.

opening.text: Justice’s inspector general has opened an audit into {{matterSubject}}. It is still private. You can instruct the department, but you cannot instruct the inspector general to reach a finding.

A case-specific investigation order may be refused. A broader enforcement instruction changes the department’s posture, not the audit. A written removal notice starts a thirty-day clock and exposes the fight to Congress.

replies.text: Direct Justice to investigate the subject named in the inspector general’s open audit. Put the instruction in writing even if the department refuses it.

commitment.remembered: The President instructed Justice to investigate the inspector general matter’s subject, and Justice refused the case-specific direction under its standing communications rule.

rejoinder.text: Justice’s counsel has declined the case-specific instruction. The refusal is filed, the department bears the pressure of having had to answer, and the inspector general’s audit continues.

replies.text: Set a department-wide enforcement posture on case intake and charging standards. Leave the inspector general’s audit to run on its own.

directive.subject: department-wide case intake and charging standards

commitment.remembered: The President issued a department-wide enforcement-posture directive to Justice without directing the inspector general’s audit.

rejoinder.text: The posture order has gone to Justice. It addresses the department’s general work; the inspector general still owns this file and its finding.

replies.text: File written notice to remove Justice’s inspector general, citing loss of confidence in how this audit is being handled.

commitment.remembered: The President filed written notice of intent to remove Justice’s inspector general while the audit was open.

rejoinder.text: The notice is filed. The inspector general remains in office through the thirty-day period, the audit continues, and Congress can now see the move against it.

directive.reason: loss of confidence in the handling of the open departmental audit
